name: Rocket Lab
one_liner: Small-satellite launcher (Electron) turned end-to-end space company building the medium-lift Neutron rocket and satellites.
story: Peter Beck founded Rocket Lab in New Zealand in 2006 and its Electron became the most-flown small launcher after SpaceX's rockets; it listed via a SPAC with Vector Acquisition in August 2021 at about a $4.1B valuation. It bought component makers and grew a spacecraft business, and by 2026 its market value was reported at $44-67B while the reusable Neutron rocket, its main bet, had still not flown and slipped toward late 2026 or 2027.

name: Relativity Space
one_liner: Rocket maker that tried to 3D-print almost an entire orbital rocket, then pivoted to the larger reusable Terran R.
story: Relativity raised $650M at a $4.2B valuation in 2021 on the idea of 3D-printing rockets; its Terran 1 reached space in March 2023 but the upper stage failed, and the company retired it to build the bigger reusable Terran R. Cash ran low while it struggled to raise more, and in 2025 former Google CEO Eric Schmidt invested, took control and replaced co-founder Tim Ellis as CEO, with Terran R aimed at a 2026 debut and about $3B in launch contracts claimed.

near_death.what: Terran 1 upper stage failed on its only flight; the rocket was cancelled
Cash reserves ran low while it failed to raise enough for Terran R; rescued by Eric Schmidt taking control in 2025

name: Firefly Aerospace
one_liner: Texas launch and lunar-lander company (Alpha rocket, Blue Ghost lander) reborn from a 2017 bankruptcy.
story: Firefly Space Systems went bankrupt in 2017, was revived by Ukrainian-born investor Max Polyakov, and in 2022 US regulators forced him to sell his stake, after which AE Industrial took control. Its Blue Ghost lander made a fully successful Moon landing in March 2025 and it listed on Nasdaq in August 2025 at about $6.3B, closing day one near $9.8B; an April 2025 Alpha launch failure and a September 2025 booster loss in testing then cut the stock about 35% in a month.

near_death.what: Firefly Space Systems filed for bankruptcy after a key investor pulled out; assets bought by Noosphere Ventures
CFIUS forced owner Max Polyakov to divest over national-security concerns
Alpha launch failure in April and a booster destroyed in a September ground test

name: ABL Space Systems (now Long Wall)
one_liner: Small-launch startup (RS1 rocket) that quit orbital launch after failures and pivoted to missile-defense test vehicles as Long Wall.
story: ABL raised nearly half a billion dollars, including a 2021 round at a $2.4B valuation, to fly the containerised RS1 rocket; its first launch failed in January 2023 and another RS1 was destroyed in a 2024 ground fire. In November 2024 it abandoned orbital launch to repurpose its rockets and ground systems for missile defense, renaming itself Long Wall in February 2025 and later unveiling an interceptor.

near_death.what: First RS1 launch failed shortly after liftoff from Kodiak, Alaska
Second RS1 destroyed in a ground fire; company exited orbital launch

name: Isar Aerospace
one_liner: Munich rocket startup building the Spectrum small launcher, Europe's best-funded private launch company.
story: Founded by Technical University of Munich graduates, Isar's first Spectrum launch from Norway in March 2025 failed about 30 seconds after liftoff. It raised a EUR150M convertible in 2025 and a EUR270M Series D in June 2026 (total about EUR870M, roughly $1B at ~1.15 USD/EUR; Bloomberg reported talks at a EUR2B valuation), and its second flight reached orbit on 5 September 2026, the first commercial orbital launch from continental Europe.

near_death.what: Maiden Spectrum flight failed about 30 seconds after liftoff

name: Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA)
one_liner: OHB-backed German small-launch company building RFA One, to fly from SaxaVord in Shetland.
story: RFA, majority-owned by satellite maker OHB, lost its first-stage test article in a fire during a static-fire test at SaxaVord in August 2024. It shipped both stages of a new RFA One to Shetland in early 2026 and targeted a summer 2026 maiden flight, but as of September 2026 it was still preparing, funded partly by ESA Boost! contracts (about EUR11.7M for two demo flights) and a shared German government commitment.

near_death.what: First stage destroyed by fire during a static-fire test on the SaxaVord pad

name: Orbex
one_liner: Scottish small-launch startup building the low-carbon Prime rocket for a UK spaceport.
story: Orbex raised about GBP138.5M (roughly $175M; GBP105M equity plus GBP33M grants) over a decade, much of it public, including GBP26M of UK government loans in 2025, but never flew its Prime rocket. After closing its Danish engine unit and cutting about 90 jobs in January 2026 and failing to close merger or takeover talks, it entered administration in February 2026 with most of its 163 staff made redundant.

name: Gilmour Space Technologies
one_liner: Australian startup building Eris, the first Australian-designed orbital rocket, and its own spaceport in Queensland.
story: Brothers Adam and James Gilmour started the company in 2012 and spent years on hybrid rocket motors and a private spaceport at Bowen, Queensland. The first Eris rocket lifted off in July 2025 and fell back about 14 seconds later; the company said it was not giving up and aimed for a second flight at the end of 2026, with trackers showing slippage into 2027.

near_death.what: Maiden Eris flight fell back to the pad area 14 seconds after liftoff

name: LandSpace
one_liner: Chinese private launcher that flew the world's first methane-fuelled rocket to orbit and is chasing reusability with Zhuque-3.
story: LandSpace's first rocket, Zhuque-1, failed in 2018 and Zhuque-2 failed on its December 2022 debut, but in July 2023 Zhuque-2 became the first methane-fuelled rocket to reach orbit, ahead of SpaceX and Blue Origin. Zhuque-3 reached orbit on its first flight in December 2025 though the booster landing failed, and the company, having raised more than 7B yuan (about $1B), filed to raise about 7.5B yuan on Shanghai's STAR Market after the exchange waived profitability rules for rocket makers; no listing was confirmed by late 2026.

near_death.what: Zhuque-1, the first orbital attempt by a Chinese private company, failed
Zhuque-2 failed on its debut before succeeding in 2023

name: Galactic Energy
one_liner: Chinese private launcher whose solid-fuel Ceres-1 became the country's most-flown commercial rocket.
story: Galactic Energy flew more than 20 successful Ceres-1 missions after its 2020 debut, but a November 2025 fourth-stage failure lost three satellites, its second failure in about two years, shortly after it raised 2.4B yuan (about $335M) and while preparing an A-share IPO. Its larger Ceres-2 failed on its January 2026 debut, and a single source reports its liquid Pallas-1 reached orbit on its first attempt in September 2026.

name: iSpace (Interstellar Glory)
one_liner: Beijing launcher that became the first Chinese private company to reach orbit, with Hyperbola-1 in 2019.
story: iSpace's solid-fuel Hyperbola-1 reached orbit in July 2019, a first for a Chinese private firm, but a string of later failures stalled it while it developed the reusable methane-fuelled Hyperbola-3. It reportedly raised a 1B yuan (about $148M) first tranche of a Series E after a large D++ round and finished IPO tutoring, targeting a STAR Market listing in the second half of 2027.

near_death.what: Two consecutive Hyperbola-1 failures after its 2019 success

name: Stoke Space
one_liner: Building Nova, a fully reusable rocket including a reusable upper stage.
story: Former Blue Origin engineers Andy Lapsa and Tom Feldman founded Stoke to make both stages of a rocket reusable, a problem even SpaceX had not solved for upper stages. It raised a $510M Series D in October 2025 led by Thomas Tull's fund (plus $100M SVB debt) and extended it to $860M in February 2026, for $1.34B raised in total; valuation was not disclosed and Nova's first launch from Cape Canaveral's LC-14 was still pending.

name: Varda Space Industries
one_liner: Makes drugs and materials in microgravity on small free-flying satellites and returns them to Earth in reentry capsules.
story: Founded by ex-SpaceX engineer Will Bruey and Founders Fund partner Delian Asparouhov, Varda's first capsule, W-1, crystallised the HIV drug ritonavir in orbit in 2023 but sat in space for months waiting for US reentry approvals before landing in Utah in February 2024. It paid the bills partly with Air Force hypersonic reentry testing, and raised a $187M Series C in 2025 and a $251M Series D at about a $1.6B valuation in 2026 (roughly $598M raised in total).

near_death.what: W-1 capsule stranded in orbit for months after the FAA denied a reentry licence; landed February 2024

name: Axiom Space
one_liner: Flies private astronaut missions to the ISS and is building a commercial space station to replace it.
story: Axiom flew four private crews to the ISS from 2022 to 2025 (Ax-4 carried astronauts from India, Poland and Hungary) and holds NASA contracts for an ISS-attached module and Artemis moonwalk suits. In 2024 it was reported to be missing supplier payments, laying off staff and cutting pay, and it went through three CEOs in about a year; it pushed its free-flying station to 2028 or later and closed a round of more than $525M in June 2026, with secondary-market valuations around $2-2.5B.

near_death.what: Reported missed supplier payments, layoffs and pay cuts; CEO Michael Suffredini stepped down

name: Vast
one_liner: Building commercial space stations (Haven-1, then Haven-2) funded largely by crypto billionaire Jed McCaleb.
story: Ripple and Stellar co-founder Jed McCaleb started Vast in 2021 and put in the bulk of more than $1B of private capital before it took outside money. It flew a Haven Demo pathfinder in late 2025, slipped Haven-1 from May 2026 to Q1 2027 for more ground testing, and in March 2026 raised $500M ($300M Series A equity plus $200M debt) to build Haven-2 as an ISS successor; valuation was not disclosed.

name: Astroscale
one_liner: Space debris removal and satellite servicing company that inspected a spent rocket stage up close in orbit.
story: Nobu Okada founded Astroscale in 2013 to clean up orbital debris, a market with no paying customer at the time; it built government demand in Japan, the UK and US and in 2024 its ADRAS-J craft approached a discarded Japanese rocket stage. It listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Growth market in June 2024, closing its first day at about 155B yen ($1B), and later traded below that (about $935M in August 2026).

name: Impulse Space
one_liner: Orbital transfer vehicles (Mira, Helios) that move satellites between orbits, founded by SpaceX's first engine chief Tom Mueller.
story: Tom Mueller, who designed SpaceX's Merlin engine, founded Impulse in 2021 to give satellites a last-mile ride between orbits. Its Mira vehicle flew three missions by 2026, and it raised a $300M Series C in June 2025 and a $500M Series D at about $4.26B in June 2026, extended by $308M in September (Series D figures from Sacra); the larger Helios stage slipped to 2027.

name: Intuitive Machines
one_liner: Lunar lander and data-relay company that made the first US Moon landing since 1972.
story: Intuitive Machines listed via a SPAC in February 2023 at about $1B; its Odysseus lander touched down near the lunar south pole in February 2024, the first US landing since Apollo, but tipped onto its side, and its second lander tipped over in a crater in March 2025. It won a NASA lunar data-relay contract worth up to $4.82B in 2024 and in January 2026 closed the $800M purchase of Lanteris (formerly Maxar's satellite unit), guiding to $920-950M of 2026 revenue.

near_death.what: Odysseus landed but tipped over, cutting the mission short
Second lander, Athena, also tipped over in a crater

name: ispace
one_liner: Japanese lunar lander company (Hakuto-R) aiming at commercial Moon delivery and resources.
story: Born from Team Hakuto in the Google Lunar XPRIZE, ispace raised a then-record $90M Series A for a Japanese startup in 2017 and listed on the Tokyo Growth market in April 2023, just before its first lander crashed on the Moon after misjudging its altitude. Its second lander, Resilience, also crashed in June 2025 after a laser rangefinder problem, and the company's market value was about 50B yen in late 2024.

near_death.what: First Hakuto-R lander crashed on the Moon weeks after the IPO
Second lander, Resilience, crashed during landing

name: Momentus
one_liner: Orbital 'space tug' startup whose SPAC listing unravelled amid SEC charges, national-security issues and failed missions.
story: Momentus promised water-plasma-powered space tugs and merged with SPAC Stable Road in 2021 at about $1.2B, but its Russian-born co-founder Mikhail Kokorich was forced out over US national-security concerns, and the SEC charged the company, Kokorich and the SPAC with misleading investors about its technology tests (settled). Its Vigoride missions underperformed, the stock lost over 99% of its value, it flagged going-concern doubts in 2025 and did a 1-for-17.85 reverse split in December 2025 while raising money in $4-5M slices.

near_death.what: SEC charges and CFIUS-driven exit of the founders during the SPAC process
Going-concern warning; reverse split to keep its Nasdaq listing

name: Masten Space Systems
one_liner: Pioneering vertical-landing rocket company that went bankrupt trying to deliver a NASA Moon lander.
story: Masten won NASA's Lunar Lander Challenge in 2009 and flew hundreds of vertical-landing test flights, then in 2020 won a $75.9M fixed-price NASA CLPS contract to land its XL-1 at the lunar south pole. Costs and delays outran the contract, and it filed for Chapter 11 in July 2022; rival Astrobotic bought its assets for about $4.5M.

name: Orbit Fab
one_liner: Building 'gas stations in space': standard refuelling ports (RAFTI) and fuel tankers for satellites.
story: Orbit Fab bet that satellites will need refuelling and sold its RAFTI docking-and-fuel port as a standard, backed largely by US Space Force and other government contracts. It raised a $28.5M Series A in 2023, cut staff that year as space funding tightened, and in 2026 reportedly named a new CEO and closed a $20M Series B, with its first operational GEO refuelling still to prove the model.

name: Starfish Space
one_liner: Builds Otter servicing spacecraft that dock with satellites to extend their life, inspect or deorbit them.
story: Founded by two ex-Blue Origin engineers, Starfish flew a small Otter Pup demonstrator in 2023 that hit thruster problems before it could dock, then rebuilt and won life-extension, inspection and deorbit contracts from commercial operators, NASA, the Space Development Agency ($52.5M) and Space Force ($54.5M). It raised $29M in 2024 and a Series B of more than $100M led by Point72 Ventures in April 2026.

name: True Anomaly
one_liner: Space-defense startup building Jackal autonomous spacecraft that approach and inspect other satellites.
story: Founded in 2022 by former US Space Force officers, True Anomaly flew its first two Jackal spacecraft in 2024 on a mission that only partly worked, then rode the defense-tech boom and the Golden Dome missile-shield push. It raised a $260M Series C led by Accel in April 2025 and, per Bloomberg, $650M at a $2.2B valuation in April 2026, taking total funding past $1B.

name: Planet Labs
one_liner: Operates the largest fleet of imaging satellites, photographing the whole Earth daily and selling the data.
story: Three ex-NASA scientists started Planet in a Cupertino garage to image the entire planet every day with shoebox-sized 'Dove' satellites, and it listed via a SPAC in December 2021 at about $2.8B. The shares sank and it cut staff in 2023 and 2024, then rallied more than 500% from early 2025 as defense and sovereign demand grew and it reached its first full year of non-GAAP profitability, with its market value reported near $10-11.5B in 2026.

near_death.what: Shares near $2 and a second round of layoffs before the 2025 rebound

name: Spire Global
one_liner: Nanosatellite data company selling weather, ship and aircraft tracking data from its own constellation.
story: Spire went public via a SPAC in 2021 at about $1.6B on the promise of selling satellite data as a subscription. By 2024-25 it had to restate several years of accounts, fell out of NYSE filing compliance, and its lender could demand repayment when buyer Kpler stalled on a deal for its maritime unit; Spire sued, and in April 2025 closed the sale for about $233.5M plus a $7.5M fee, using it to retire all its debt.

near_death.what: Accounting restatement, NYSE non-compliance and a stalled asset sale with debt callable; rescued by closing the $233.5M maritime sale

name: BlackSky Technology
one_liner: Runs a constellation of small high-revisit imaging satellites plus AI analytics sold mainly to defense and intelligence agencies.
story: BlackSky went public through a merger with Osprey Technology Acquisition Corp in 2021 and sold rapid-revisit imagery and AI-based monitoring mostly to the US government and allies. Like other 2021 space SPACs its shares fell heavily, and it bet on a third-generation satellite fleet starting in 2025 to win larger defense contracts.

name: Satellogic
one_liner: Argentine-founded maker and operator of low-cost sub-metre imaging satellites.
story: Emiliano Kargieman founded Satellogic in Buenos Aires in 2010 to build cheap imaging satellites in-house, and it listed via a SPAC with Cantor's CF Acquisition Corp V in January 2022 at about $850M. The stock collapsed with other space SPACs, it later moved its legal home to the US to chase American defense work, and analysts still call it a speculative stock with small revenue.

name: ICEYE
one_liner: Finnish operator of the largest synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) small-satellite constellation, imaging through clouds and at night.
story: Two Aalto University students started ICEYE in 2014 to shrink radar satellites, which most experts thought too power-hungry for small spacecraft. Wartime demand after Russia's invasion of Ukraine turned it into Europe's defense-intelligence darling: it raised at about EUR2.4B in December 2025 and then a EUR450M primary Series F (over EUR1B with secondaries) led by General Atlantic in June 2026 at more than EUR10B (about $11.5B), roughly quadrupling in six months.

name: Capella Space
one_liner: US synthetic-aperture radar satellite operator, bought by quantum-computing company IonQ.
story: Payam Banazadeh founded Capella in 2016 to build high-resolution commercial radar satellites for US defense and commercial customers. IonQ agreed in May 2025 to buy it in a mostly-stock deal valued at about $318M at signing to build space-based quantum networking; by the July 2025 close IonQ's rising share price lifted the consideration to about $424.8M ($48.3M cash plus $376.5M stock).

name: Pixxel
one_liner: Indian startup running a hyperspectral imaging satellite constellation that sees hundreds of colour bands.
story: Founded by two BITS Pilani students in 2019, Pixxel launched six Firefly hyperspectral satellites from 2025, claiming the highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral constellation. It raised a $36M Series B led by Google in 2023 and a $100M Series C led by Temasek and Seraphim in September 2026, India's largest space-tech round, for about $195M in total; valuation was not disclosed.

name: Albedo
one_liner: Tried to sell airplane-quality 10 cm satellite imagery from very low Earth orbit, then pivoted to selling VLEO satellite buses.
story: Albedo raised $97M to fly satellites low enough (very low Earth orbit) to capture 10 cm visible imagery, a resolution previously limited to aircraft and spy satellites. Its first satellite, Clarity-1, launched in March 2025 and went into a protective mode after first contact; per Wikipedia it lacked thrust, decayed and reentered in June 2026, and the company pivoted to building VLEO satellite buses for other operators.

name: AST SpaceMobile
one_liner: Building giant satellites that connect directly to ordinary unmodified smartphones (space-based cellular broadband).
story: Abel Avellan founded AST in 2017 to beam broadband from huge phased-array satellites straight to normal phones, an idea many in the industry doubted, and it listed via a SPAC in 2021. After its BlueWalker 3 prototype in 2022, its shares sank in early 2024 amid funding worries until AT&T, Google and Vodafone invested; the first five BlueBird satellites launched in September 2024 and the stock became one of the biggest space winners as direct-to-cell rivals such as Starlink and Lynk raced in.

near_death.what: Shares fell sharply on cash worries before strategic investment from AT&T, Google and Vodafone

name: Lynk Global
one_liner: Pioneered satellite-to-ordinary-phone texting, then merged with Omnispace after a failed SPAC to form Elveo Mobile.
story: Lynk sent what it called the first text from a satellite to a standard phone and signed dozens of mobile operators, but as SpaceX's Starlink and AST SpaceMobile moved into direct-to-cell, its 2024 SPAC deal with Slam Corp dragged on and was cancelled amid a legal dispute. In October 2025 it agreed to merge with SES-backed Omnispace, and the combined company closed in August 2026 as Elveo Mobile.

name: Project Kuiper (Amazon Leo)
one_liner: Amazon's in-house low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation, the main well-funded challenger to Starlink.
story: Amazon announced Project Kuiper in 2019, won FCC approval for 3,236 satellites in 2020 on condition that half be launched by mid-2026, and committed more than $10B. It flew prototypes in 2023 and its first production satellites in April 2025, then rebranded the service Amazon Leo in late 2025; it is context for any satellite-broadband startup, since it shows the capital a late entrant needs even with a trillion-dollar parent.

name: Terran Orbital
one_liner: Small-satellite manufacturer that listed via SPAC, booked a giant constellation order that never paid, and was sold cheaply to Lockheed Martin.
story: Terran Orbital built small satellites for the US military and went public via SPAC in 2022 at about $1.58B, then announced a $2.4B order for 300 satellites from Rivada that depended on Rivada raising funds it never secured. Burning cash and carrying heavy debt, it was bought by its biggest customer and shareholder Lockheed Martin in October 2024 for about $450M including debt, roughly $0.25 a share.

name: Apex
one_liner: Mass-produces standardized satellite buses so customers can buy a spacecraft off the shelf instead of custom-building it.
story: Apex was founded in 2022 to turn satellite buses, traditionally custom-built over years, into a standard product shipped in months, and flew its first bus within about two years. Riding US defense constellation demand, it raised $200M at a $2.3B valuation in June 2026; a single aggregator reports a later $500M round at $4B that is unconfirmed.

name: K2 Space
one_liner: Builds very large, high-power satellite buses designed for the cheap heavy-lift launch era.
story: Brothers Karan and Neel Kunjur left SpaceX in 2022 betting that Starship-class launch would make big, powerful satellites cheap to fly, so the bottleneck would become the satellites themselves. Its valuation went from about $1.5B in February 2025 to $3B with a $250M Series C in December 2025 and $6.8B with a $500M Series D co-led by Kleiner Perkins and ICONIQ in July 2026, taking funding to about $1B.

name: Commonwealth Fusion Systems
one_liner: MIT spinout building compact tokamak fusion reactors using high-temperature superconducting magnets.
story: CFS spun out of MIT in 2018 and in 2021 demonstrated a 20-tesla high-temperature superconducting magnet, then raised $1.8B, the largest private fusion round at the time. It added $863M in 2025 and about $1B more in July 2026 (roughly $4B in total; one profile cites a larger 2026 figure that could not be reconciled), signed power deals with Google and Eni for its planned ARC plant in Virginia, and targets net energy from its SPARC device in 2027.

name: Helion
one_liner: Pulsed magneto-inertial fusion company that promised Microsoft fusion electricity by 2028.
story: Helion signed the first fusion power purchase agreement in 2023, promising Microsoft electricity by 2028, and began building its Orion plant in Malaga, Washington in 2025 though no fusion device anywhere had yet produced net electricity. Backed by Sam Altman, it raised $425M at about $5.2B in January 2025 and a $465M Series G led by Thrive Capital at $15.5B in June 2026 (about $1.5B raised), reporting deuterium-tritium operation of its Polaris prototype.

name: TAE Technologies
one_liner: Decades-old private fusion company (hydrogen-boron) that agreed to merge with Trump Media in 2025.
story: Founded in 1998 as Tri Alpha Energy, TAE spent more than two decades and over $1.3B from backers including Google and Chevron pursuing aneutronic hydrogen-boron fusion without a commercial reactor. In December 2025 it agreed to an all-stock merger with Donald Trump's loss-making Trump Media & Technology Group valuing the combined company at more than $6B, with each side owning about half and Trump Media advancing up to $300M in cash; it planned to start building its first plant in 2026.

name: General Fusion
one_liner: Canadian magnetized-target fusion pioneer that nearly ran out of money in 2025 after two decades of work.

rounds.lead: SPAC: Spring Valley Acquisition Corp III (announced)

story: Founded in 2002 and backed by Jeff Bezos, General Fusion raised about $440M but in May 2025 its CEO published an open letter citing an 'unexpected and urgent financing constraint', laid off about a quarter of its 140 staff, scaled back its LM26 machine and sought $125M. A $22M lifeline kept it alive, and it then announced a reverse merger with SPAC Spring Valley III valuing the combined company at about $1B with up to $335M in proceeds; completion was not confirmed in the sources.

near_death.what: Open letter on an urgent financing gap, ~25% layoffs and LM26 scaled back; saved by a $22M lifeline and a SPAC deal

name: Zap Energy
one_liner: Pursues a magnet-free sheared-flow Z-pinch fusion design aimed at cheaper, smaller reactors.
story: Zap spun out of University of Washington research to skip the giant magnets most fusion designs need, using a sheared-flow Z-pinch instead. It raised a $160M Series C and later a $130M round disclosed in an SEC filing, about $327M in total per PitchBook, while working toward scientific breakeven.

name: Tokamak Energy
one_liner: UK spherical-tokamak fusion company that also sells its high-temperature superconducting magnet technology.
story: Spun out of the UK's Culham fusion lab ecosystem in 2009, Tokamak Energy built compact spherical tokamaks and reached 100 million degrees in its ST40 device in 2022. To fund a long road to power plants, it split out a business selling high-temperature superconducting magnets for other uses and raised $125M in late 2024.

name: Marvel Fusion
one_liner: German laser-driven fusion startup using nanostructured fuel targets and short-pulse lasers.
story: Marvel Fusion bets that ultra-short laser pulses on nanostructured targets can trigger fusion without the huge facilities of government laser labs. Backed by Siemens Energy Ventures and Deutsche Telekom among others, it raised a Series B in 2025 (totals reported at roughly $160-208M) and is building a demonstration facility with Colorado State University for 2027.

name: Oklo
one_liner: Advanced fast-reactor company (Aurora powerhouse) backed by Sam Altman, listed via his SPAC.
story: Oklo's first licence application was denied by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission in 2022 for missing information, yet it listed in May 2024 via AltC, the SPAC co-led by Sam Altman, with no reactor built and no revenue. AI data-center power hype sent the stock up more than 1,000% from early 2024 at one point in 2025; in 2026 the market cap was around $10-11B, still without an operating plant.

near_death.what: NRC denied its first combined licence application for the Aurora reactor

name: NuScale Power
one_liner: Small modular reactor developer with the first US NRC-approved SMR design.
story: NuScale spun out of Oregon State University in 2007, became the first SMR design certified by the NRC, and listed via SPAC in 2022 at about $1.9B. Its flagship Utah project with UAMPS was cancelled in November 2023 when estimated power prices rose and utilities pulled out; after an uprated design approval in 2025 and a 6GW agreement involving TVA the stock soared, then fell nearly 80% from its July 2025 high to about a $3.6-4B market cap in 2026.

near_death.what: First customer project (UAMPS Carbon Free Power Project) cancelled; layoffs followed

name: Kairos Power
one_liner: Builds fluoride-salt-cooled advanced reactors; signed the first corporate SMR deal with Google.
story: Founded by UC Berkeley nuclear engineers, Kairos took an iterative, build-and-test approach and won NRC construction permits for its Hermes test reactors in Oak Ridge, Tennessee in 2023 and 2024. In October 2024 Google agreed to buy up to 500MW from Kairos reactors by 2035, the first corporate deal of its kind; its funding has been largely undisclosed.

name: X-energy
one_liner: High-temperature gas-cooled small reactor and TRISO fuel developer backed by Amazon.
story: X-energy agreed in 2022 to go public via Ares Acquisition Corp at about $2B, but the SPAC deal was terminated in 2023 amid tough markets. It won US Department of Energy demonstration funding for a plant with Dow in Texas and in October 2024 raised a $500M Series C-1 anchored by Amazon, which plans to use its reactors.

near_death.what: $2B SPAC merger with Ares Acquisition Corp terminated

name: Last Energy
one_liner: Builds small, factory-made pressurized-water microreactors for industrial and data-center customers.
story: Founded by Bret Kugelmass, Last Energy shrinks conventional pressurized-water reactor technology into 20MW units built in factories, initially pitching European customers. It raised $40M in 2024 ($64M total) and a $100M+ Series C led by the Astera Institute in December 2025, aiming for its PWR-5 pilot at Texas A&M to go critical in 2026.

name: Newcleo
one_liner: Lead-cooled small fast reactors that run on recycled nuclear waste fuel.
story: Founded in London in 2021 by physicist-entrepreneur Stefano Buono and later headquartered in Paris, Newcleo raised hundreds of millions of euros unusually early (totals reported at EUR487-645M) and was valued at about EUR1.5B in 2024 (about $1.6B). It raised a EUR75M (about $88M) Series B in early 2026 and was reported to be pursuing a Nasdaq listing through a SPAC at about $2.4B, a figure not confirmed by primary sources.
